title: Course Logistics and Setup
markdown:
## What this covers

STAT 243 runs its non-lecture requirements — in-class assessments, a project, and the software
setup a student needs before the technical material starts — on a fixed pattern that repeats each
time the course is offered, with small changes in naming and dates from year to year. This chapter
lays out that pattern, drawn from the "Scheduling information" page published for the fall 2024,
fall 2025 and fall 2026 offerings. It assumes only that the reader is enrolled in, or considering,
the course; it does not require anything from the statistical-computing material itself.

## In-class assessments

Every offering gives two in-class, in-person written assessments during the term, each preceded by
a review session held in section a few days beforehand. The name attached to them has changed
across offerings — they were "quizzes" in fall 2024, "mini-exams" in fall 2025, and "243A exam" /
"243B exam" in fall 2026 — but the structure is the same in each case: one assessment roughly seven
weeks into the term (mid-to-late October) and a second about a month later (late November), neither
of them take-home or online.

For example, in fall 2024 the first quiz split students by last name across two rooms (Evans 60 for
A–T, Evans 340 for V–Z) and was preceded by a review session in section five days earlier; the
second quiz followed the same pattern about five weeks later. Fall 2025 kept the same two-assessment
timing but dropped the room split. Fall 2026 renamed the two assessments after the course's A/B
structure (243A, 243B) rather than calling them quizzes or mini-exams.

## The project

Fall 2024 and fall 2025 both list a course project due during exam week, with the exact date left
"TBD" on the schedule page and presumably fixed later in the term once the rest of the syllabus is
set. The fall 2026 schedule page (as converted) does not mention a project.

## Setup: the optional help session and the first lab

Before the technical material starts, the course runs an optional help session — Lab 0 in fall 2024
and fall 2025, Lab A0 in fall 2026 — for installing the required software, getting access to a
Unix-style command line, and working through a basic command-line tutorial. Unlike every later lab,
a student can walk in at any point during this session rather than only at its start. The
expectation is that software is installed and the command line is at least minimally familiar
*before* the first regular class meeting of the following week.

The first regular lab (Lab 1, or Lab A1 in fall 2026) then covers three things a student will use
for the rest of the term: Git, setting up the GitHub repository that problem sets are submitted
through, and Quarto for producing dynamic documents. Because room space is limited, students are
asked to attend only the section they are registered for, unless they have arranged otherwise with
the instructor.

## Preparatory tutorials: the shell, and (in some years) regular expressions

Alongside the labs, the course assigns a self-study tutorial on using the bash shell, to be worked
through by a fixed date early in the term (September 9 in fall 2024, September 8 in fall 2025).
Students read the tutorial — skipping the sections on regular expressions and on managing processes
— and then submit answers to the first ten problems in the accompanying exercise set through
Gradescope. This is explicitly not graded as a formal problem set: no particular format or
commentary is expected, submissions need not go in the student's GitHub repository, and even a
scanned handwritten answer is acceptable. The point is only to confirm the tutorial was worked
through, ahead of the instructor's own command-line demonstrations that begin in class the same
week.

Fall 2024 additionally assigned a second, separate tutorial and exercise set on regular expressions,
due a few days after the bash shell tutorial (by September 13), again submitted on Gradescope and
marked only as completed or not rather than graded in the usual sense. The fall 2025 and fall 2026
schedule pages, as converted here, do not carry this separate regular-expressions assignment.

## LaTeX for typesetting mathematics

Every offering recommends — but does not require — an optional library session on writing
mathematics in LaTeX, aimed particularly at Statistics graduate students. The point made each year
is the same: even a student who writes their documents in Quarto, Jupyter notebooks or R Markdown
rather than in a LaTeX document will still typeset equations using LaTeX's math syntax, since that
syntax is the common tool those other formats render through.

## Sources

- `berkeley-stat243/fall-2024/schedule.md` ("Scheduling information" page, converted from
  `schedule.qmd`) — quiz dates and rooms, project due date, Lab 0/Lab 1 descriptions, bash shell
  tutorial deadline, and the separate regular-expressions tutorial assignment.
- `berkeley-stat243/fall-2025/schedule.md` — mini-exam dates, project due date, Lab 0/Lab 1
  descriptions, and the bash shell tutorial deadline (no separate regex assignment on this page).
- `berkeley-stat243/fall-2026/schedule.md` — 243A/243B exam dates, Lab A0/Lab A1 descriptions (no
  project or bash-tutorial deadline given on this page).

All three pages are administrative "scheduling information" pages from the course website rather
than lecture material; no slides, transcript or problem set were supplied for this chapter, and no
technical statistical-computing content appears in the source pages themselves.
